title: From task-specific networks to foundation models in diabetes care: a critical review of opportunities, evaluation gaps, and safety frontiers.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Artificial intelligence in diabetes care has historically relied on task-specific supervised learning, such as bespoke networks for retinopathy grading, kidney disease prediction, and glucose forecasting. The emergence of foundation models (FMs: large models pretrained on broad data, typically with self-supervision, and adapted to many downstream tasks) is displacing this paradigm across diabetes-relevant modalities: ophthalmic models such as RETFound, pretrained on 1.6 million retinal photographs, have been reported to outperform task-specific networks on retinopathy grading and systemic disease prediction, especially when labeled data are scarce; transformer-based time-series models are replacing long short-term memory (LSTM) pipelines for continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) forecasting; clinical large language models (LLMs) such as Med-PaLM and GPT-4 attain expert-level scores on medical question-answering benchmarks; and generative models supply synthetic CGM and electronic health record (EHR) data. This review provides a critical, modality-organized synthesis of this transition. We (i) formalize a three-era taxonomy: rule-based risk scores (era I), task-specific deep learning (era II, 2016-2020), and foundation models (era III, from 2021), and map the diabetes literature onto it; (ii) survey foundation-model architectures, pretraining objectives, and adaptation strategies across retinal imaging, CGM, longitudinal EHR, and multimodal data; (iii) expose an evaluation crisis: benchmark contamination of LLM medical evaluations, a near-universal absence in the literature we reviewed of external and prospective validation for retinal and CGM foundation models, miscalibration under dataset shift, and, to our knowledge and within the reviewed literature (January 2016-December 2025; negative findings are time-sensitive), the absence of any randomized evaluation of a foundation model in a diabetes workflow; and (iv) analyze safety risks: hallucinated insulin-dosing advice, automation bias, inherited algorithmic inequity, and privacy exposure during adaptation. We conclude that the decisive open problem is no longer representation learning but grounded, calibrated, causally informed deployment, requiring contamination-resistant evaluation, prospective trials, and hybrid architectures coupling foundation-model representations with treatment-effect estimation.

title: Causally Constrained and Uncertainty-Aware Cardiopulmonary Risk Prediction
desc: Routine chest computed tomography (CT) captures pulmonary, cardiac, and vascular phenotypes that jointly stratify lung cancer and cardiovascular disease, the two leading causes of death in lung-screening populations. Yet clinical risk calculators evaluate each disease in isolation and omit CT findings, whereas unconstrained machine learning overfits small hospital cohorts, learns treatment- and illness-confounded risk directions, and conceals uncertainty when patient records are incomplete. Here we present the Causal Envelope Agent (CE-Agent), a two-stage framework that compiles peer-reviewed epidemiological evidence into explicit constraints on risk-factor weights before any outcome is seen, while estimating local baseline risk and newly added CT phenotypes from cohort data. At deployment, closed-form uncertainty propagation accounts for missing clinical or CT inputs within milliseconds per patient, running over two orders of magnitude faster than Monte Carlo sampling and returning calibrated risk intervals that direct chart review and selective imaging to borderline patients. Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, CE-Agent outperforms cardiovascular calculators in lung screening, exceeds the Pooled Cohort Equations on hard atherosclerotic events while correcting their 1.7-fold risk overestimation, and generalizes from a single hospital or CT scanner to external sites while lowering required sample sizes up to fivefold. Applied unchanged to lung cancer, CE-Agent matches established screening models with accurate calibration even when restricted to risk-factor directions alone, and pairing both predictions improves joint cardiopulmonary triage from a single screening visit.

title: LabARIA: A Multi-Agent System for Integrative Analytics in Clinical Laboratories
desc: Background Laboratory medicine underpins clinical decision-making across nearly every care setting. Clinical laboratory errors and delays can compromise diagnostic reliability and patient care. However, laboratory quality and operational data are commonly reviewed through separate manual workflows, limiting timely recognition of emerging problems across complementary data sources. Methods We developed and evaluated LabARIA (Laboratory Agentic Reasoning and Integrative Analytics), a multi-agent AI system for coordinated surveillance of specimen workflows, analytical quality control, and laboratory operations. We conducted a single-center retrospective system development and evaluation at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital/Weill Cornell Medical Center using laboratory data collected from May 1 through June 18, 2026, including 177,480 specimen-panel records, 75,103 internal quality-control (IQC) measurements, 633 proficiency-testing challenges, and 422 recalibration or maintenance actions. Forecasting agents were evaluated using patient-result streams with controlled perturbations, and synthetic staffing and inventory data. We assessed specimen rejection, cancellation, and turnaround-time patterns; warning recall and lead time before documented laboratory actions; assay-specific patient-based real-time quality control (PBRTQC) performance; and exploratory operational forecasting discrimination. Findings LabARIA characterized specimen and workflow patterns across clinical units and time periods, including hemolysis-related potassium rejections in the intensive care unit during early morning hours (49 of 367 tests [13.3%]). For analytical quality monitoring, the IQC agent generated warnings before 407 of 422 recorded QC actions (recall, 0.964 [95% CI, 0.942-0.978]), with a median lead time of 5.40 days (95% CI, 3.75-6.07). PBRTQC agent selected different monitoring strategies across 35 analytes. In a separate analysis, adding PBRTQC increased action recall from 0.964 to 0.993 (95% CI, 0.979-0.998). A dashboard presented tiered alerts for human review, and an accompanying chatbot supported interactive exploration of the summaries. For the operational forecasting module, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve for 7-day inventory and staffing risk forecasting were 0.800 (95% CI, 0.696-0.881) and 0.877 (95% CI, 0.778-0.950), respectively. title: Inferring single-cell gene expression profiles from multicellular spatial transcriptomics data with st2sc
desc: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables the quantitative measurement of gene expression within tissue sections but is currently limited in spatial resolution, as each spot aggregates signals from multiple cells. Recovering single-cell gene expression profiles from these multicellular measurements requires two steps: explicit identification of individual cells and accurate estimation of per-gene expression. While existing methods have demonstrated the feasibility of recovering single-cell expression profiles, accurately estimating gene-level expression for individual cells remains an important challenge. To address this challenge, we propose st2sc (Spatial Transcriptomics to Single-Cell), an end-to-end framework for inferring single-cell gene profiles from multicellular ST data. st2sc introduces a novel Attention Gradient Flow Tracking (AGFT) algorithm that extracts attention maps from a Vision-Gene Transformer to identify candidate cell instances without predefined background constraints. The detected instances are then used by a set of regressors trained under a multiple-instance, multiple-target regression setting to predict precise single-cell gene expression counts. Comprehensive evaluations on synthetic and Visium-like datasets demonstrate that st2sc significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accurately segmenting cellular instances and predicting gene counts. The method can further resolve contested 2um bin in Visium HD. Application to human IPF lung showed the model can recover the subtype marker level analysis. This advancement further improves single-cell resolution analysis in spatial transcriptomics, facilitating more accurate downstream biological analyses.

Artificial Intelligence in Valvular Heart Disease: Imaging, Quantification, Risk Prediction, and Potential Clinical Decision Support.
desc: [Methodist DeBakey cardiovascular journal] Valvular heart disease (VHD) affects a substantial proportion of the population and remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality worldwide. Despite advances in surgical and transcatheter therapies, important challenges persist. VHD remains underdiagnosed, assessment of disease severity is often variable, and the optimal timing of intervention continues to evolve. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool across the spectrum of VHD care. AI-based electrocardiogram analysis can identify both existing and future VHD, while AI-guided point-of-care ultrasound extends screening to nonspecialist settings. Across multimodality imaging, machine learning (ML) and deep learning algorithms enable automated, reproducible assessment of VHD. In echocardiography, AI supports grading of disease severity across the main valvular lesions, including Doppler interpretation and automated report generation. AI-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance facilitates automated assessment of ventricular remodeling and myocardial fibrosis, while AI-assisted cardiac computed tomography improves procedural planning for transcatheter interventions. In parallel, ML has identified distinct patient phenotypes in multiple valvular lesions with differing clinical trajectories and responses to intervention. This review summarizes current applications of AI in detection, multimodality imaging, and potential clinical decision support for VHD and discusses opportunities and challenges for integration into routine practice.

title: A thorough review on Deep Learning approaches to 2D-to-3D Registration in Medical Imaging
desc: 2D-to-3D image registration is a key component for several medical imaging purposes such as intraoperative guidance, enabling the alignment between preoperative 3D volumes and real-time 2D images. While conventional optimisation-based methods often struggle with non-convex objectives, sensitivity to initialisation, and high computational demands, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising alternative, offering improved alignment robustness and the potential for real-time performance. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of DL frameworks developed to address the challenges inherent in 2D-to-3D registration. We first outline how core concepts of DL are adapted to the registration problem. We then examine recent methodological advancements from multiple perspectives, including pipeline design, architectural innovations, and domain adaptation strategies. Particular attention is given to quantitative metrics, highlighting how performance is defined and measured across studies. Across the 41 included studies, we find that direct regression is the most common pipeline (23 studies, against 18 iterative ones), that hybrid CNN-attention architectures are gaining ground, and that research remains heavily concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration. We conclude by identifying the absence of per-case uncertainty estimation and the strong neglect of temporal or sequential modelling as the two methodological gaps most consequential for clinical readiness, and discuss state-space models as a way to add temporal memory within intraoperative latency budgets. Further opportunities lie in more principled domain adaptation and in the integration of foundation models for representation learning.

title: Effect of Data Preprocessing Decisions on Sepsis-3 Labels in MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD: A Sensitivity Analysis
desc: Objective: Published Sepsis-3 detection rates range from 3.4 % to 65.2 % in MIMIC-III and from 9.8 % to 47.9 % in eICU-CRD. We tested whether data preprocessing decisions alone produce differences of this magnitude when data, cohort and sepsis definition are held fixed. Materials and Methods: Using the MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD databases we developed and applied a configurable pipeline (medalabel) that stepwise maps the databases into the OMOP Common Data Model, standardizes and cleans the data, and preprocesses them to compute Sepsis-3 labels. Each setting of the preprocessing represents one decision of published Sepsis-3 implementations, and settings can be freely combined. On fixed cohorts of first ICU stays (13,388 in MIMIC-III, 94,782 in eICU-CRD), we changed one setting of a reference configuration at a time (51 variants in five preprocessing domains) and compared detection rates and septic stays (Jaccard index) with the reference. We approximately reconstructed six published pipelines and combined the settings with the largest effects in pairs to test whether their effects add up. The time a value is measured can differ from the time it is documented and thus available for automated analysis. Beyond the usual retrospective view based on measurement time, the pipeline optionally combines both time points to simulate a real-time system. Results: The reference configuration labelled 31.5 % of ICU stays in MIMIC-III and 8.2 % in eICU-CRD as septic. Changing a single setting resulted in sepsis detection rates of 15.3-58.6 % in MIMIC-III and 4.6-17.2 % in eICU-CRD. The largest shifts from the reference, all in the same direction in both databases, came from the SOFA baseline, up to +27.1 percentage points (pp) in MIMIC-III and +9.0 pp in eICU-CRD, from disabling imputation (-16.3 and -2.5 pp), the temporal window (+12.6 and +5.3 pp) and aggregation (-10.1 and -0.8 pp); clinician-validated parameter sets had little effect (-4.8 and -1.1 pp). Even variants that changed the rate by less than 2 pp labelled partly different patients, with Jaccard indices as low as 0.67 in MIMIC-III and 0.56 in eICU-CRD (1 = identical septic stays). Reconstructions deviated from the published rates by 2-10 pp. Two settings applied together deviated from the sum of their single effects by 0.9-11.8 pp in MIMIC-III and by up to 4.9 pp in eICU-CRD. Current Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Surgical Planning for Craniosynostosis: A Scoping Review.
desc: [ANZ journal of surgery] Craniosynostosis, the premature fusion of cranial sutures, can cause abnormal skull shapes, neurological issues and aesthetic concerns. Surgical correction is standard, but planning is complex and operator-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers the potential to enhance diagnosis, optimise planning and predict postoperative outcomes. A scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines identified 11 studies involving paediatric patients with craniosynostosis. AI methods included unsupervised machine learning, convolutional neural networks, finite element models and variational autoencoders. Applications encompassed cranial severity scoring, phenotype classification, preoperative surgical simulation, intraoperative guidance and outcome prediction. AI-derived metrics correlated strongly with expert assessments, facilitated patient-specific planning and predicted postoperative aesthetics. AI is a transformative adjunct in craniosynostosis surgery. Clinically, it improves diagnostic accuracy, supports personalised surgical planning and guides intraoperative decision-making. Some studies show AI can contribute to better functional and aesthetic outcomes, showing great promise in the paediatric surgical field. Although AI does not replace clinical expertise, it enhances precision and reproducibility. Future research should prioritise prospective validation, integration into surgical workflows and development of interpretable, surgeon-friendly AI tools to maximise clinical benefit.

title: A Tumour-Aware Multimodal Framework for Explainable Prediction of IDH Mutation in Gliomas from Multi-Sequence MRI
desc: Accurate prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status is essential for glioma diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. Although recent deep learning approaches have demonstrated promising performance, many rely on whole-brain feature extraction and provide limited interpretability. This study proposes a tumour-aware multimodal framework for explainable, non-invasive prediction of IDH mutation status from multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The proposed framework integrates four MRI sequences (T1, T1CE, T2, and FLAIR), tumour subregion segmentation, quantitative radiomic descriptors, and clinical information within a unified deep learning architecture. An ablation study was conducted to evaluate the contribution of tumour-aware learning, radiomic features, and clinical variables. Model performance was assessed using multiple complementary evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, balanced accuracy, receiver operating characteristic analysis, confusion matrix evaluation, and Grad-CAM visualisation. Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed multimodal framework consistently outperformed the baseline MRI-only model, with the Clinical Fusion model achieving the strongest overall predictive performance. The integration of tumour-aware learning, radiomic descriptors, and clinical information progressively improved classification performance, while Grad-CAM visualisations indicated that the model predominantly focused on biologically relevant tumour regions. These findings suggest that tumour-aware multimodal feature integration enables accurate, interpretable, and non-invasive molecular profiling of gliomas and provides a promising foundation for future clinical decision support in precision neuro-oncology.

Artificial intelligence for precision nephrology: current evidence to clinical translation and future prospects.
desc: [Frontiers in nephrology] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across nephrology, with potential applications spanning disease prediction, diagnosis, treatment optimisation, and clinical decision support. However, reported model performance varies substantially across clinical domains, and high predictive performance does not necessarily demonstrate clinical utility or readiness for deployment. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the applications of AI in nephrology and critically evaluates the methodological maturity, validation, interpretability, fairness, and translational readiness of AI systems across major nephrology domains. A structured literature search of PubMed was conducted using terms related to AI and nephrology, with the primary eligibility period restricted to studies published from 2020 to 2025. The search strategy incorporated artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, natural language processing, large language models, generative AI, computer vision, reinforcement learning, federated learning, and related terms, together with nephrology and kidney-disease terms. Title/abstract and full-text screening were performed independently by the first and second authors, with disagreements resolved by the third author. Two foundational pre-2020 studies identified through citation chaining were retained because of their importance to the subsequent development of AI applications in nephrology. Evidence was synthesized qualitatively according to study design, validation, predictive performance, interpretability, fairness, prospective evaluation, and translational readiness. AI applications were identified across acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, nephropathology, kidney transplantation, haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, large language models, reinforcement learning, and federated learning. Across these domains, many models demonstrated promising discrimination, but evidence maturity varied considerably. External validation was present for some applications, whereas prospective evaluation and evidence of clinical utility remained limited. The literature also highlighted challenges related to calibration, generalizability, interpretability, algorithmic fairness, data governance, and integration into clinical workflows. title: Cracks in Embeddings: Robustness and Stability of JEPA-Based Chest X-Ray Representations
desc: Self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models are increasingly used for medical imaging, however there is a limited understanding about robustness of these models toward real-world image changes. We test four JEPA-based chest X-ray encoders, trained on 78,468 NIH ChestX-ray14 images, under six tests: two black-box adversarial attacks (SPSA, Boundary Attack), three image corruptions (Gaussian noise, brightness shift, contrast shift), and a label-scarcity test, measuring embedding change and classification AUROC. These perturbations cause severe, model-dependent damage: encoder-level Cosine Similarity drops as low as 0.33, and AUROC falls by as much as 0.12 in the worst case (I-JEPA under the Boundary Test). We test two ways of training the small predictor on top of each frozen encoder to address this. Adversarial fine-tuning, trained on clean and perturbed images together, raises embedding consistency above 0.97 in nearly every case and improves AUROC, relative to the same perturbed baseline, for most models, with the largest gain of $+0.10$ on I-JEPA. A Vector-Quantized codebook method, trained only on clean images and evaluated on perturbed test images for the first time, instead degrades under distortion for all four models, most noticeably for I-JEPA ($-0.15$ AUROC on average), showing that its discrete bottleneck alone does not provide the robustness that comes from training on perturbed data directly.

Toward precision nanomedicine via artificial intelligence guided design and prediction.
desc: [Advanced drug delivery reviews] Artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing nanomedicine development by linking formulation variables and biological context with delivery, therapeutic efficacy, and safety. This review examines AI assisted formulation design, centralized formulation databases, prediction of nanoparticle self assembly, and models of cell and tissue selective delivery, biodistribution, and therapeutic outcomes. Recent advances in predicting nanotoxicity and nanoparticle induced immune responses further emphasize the importance of incorporating safety endpoints into nanomedicine optimization. Beyond nanocarrier engineering, foundation models and multimodal analyses of single-cell and spatial data are expanding biological discovery by characterizing disease associated cellular states, prioritizing therapeutic targets, and predicting treatment responses. Computational approaches also support the design of therapeutic RNA, peptides, proteins, and programmable protein nanomaterials. For example, mRNA sequences generated by GEMORNA and delivered via lipid nanoparticles increased erythropoietin expression in mice by up to 15-fold compared with a benchmark sequence. Integration of biological discovery with biomolecular and nanocarrier design may inform therapeutic cargo selection, targeting strategies, and functional nanomaterial development. AI may connect patient specific biological characteristics with predictions of nanomedicine delivery and therapeutic response to support patient stratification and individualized treatment selection. Integration of histological, imaging, molecular, and longitudinal data may enable treatment strategies to be adapted to differences in tissue characteristics, disease state, and therapeutic response. Emerging approaches based on digital twins and adaptive treatment control may extend the framework toward individualized dosing and dynamic treatment optimization. Major challenges include data heterogeneity, limited model generalizability, and the need for experimental and prospective validation. Progress toward precision therapy will require integrated frameworks that jointly consider delivery, efficacy, selectivity, and safety while clearly distinguishing demonstrated applications from future opportunities.

title: PADSNet: Physics-Aware Dual-Stream Network with Biomechanical Priors for Laryngeal Lesion Classification
desc: Precise classification of laryngeal lesions is clinically crucial yet highly challenging, as inter-class visual differences are often subtle. While abnormalities in vocal fold vibratory dynamics provide complementary discriminative information, existing deep learning models predominantly rely on visual appearance and lack explicit mechanisms for modeling clinically meaningful vibratory dynamics. To address this, we propose PADSNet, a Physics-Aware Dual-Stream Network for laryngeal lesion classification that integrates visual representations with explicit biomechanical reasoning. Specifically, a Wavelet-Attention Enhancement Module (WAEM) is designed to bridge the spectral-semantic gap, enabling complementary learning of spatial texture and dynamic frequency representations. Meanwhile, a Knowledge Computing Module (KCM) extracts interpretable biomechanical indices from temporal glottal distance waveforms, including indicators of mobility, symmetry, glottal closure, and vibration stability. These descriptors are subsequently incorporated into a Physics-Aware Gating Module (PAGM) as biomechanical priors to adaptively recalibrate visual feature toward pathology-relevant vibratory patterns. Extensive experiments on a clinical dataset demonstrate that PADSNet achieves an accuracy of 0.8452, an F1-score of 0.8090, a sensitivity of 0.7953, and a specificity of 0.8866. These results indicate that explicitly integrating biomechanical priors with deep visual representations provides a more accurate, robust, and clinically interpretable framework for automated laryngeal lesion classification.

AI-enabled drug repurposing in Alzheimer's disease: from computational nomination to pharmacological proof.
desc: [Frontiers in pharmacology] Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded the scale and speed of drug repurposing in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Transcriptomic signature matching, network-based systems pharmacology, real-world data pharmacoepidemiology and multi-omics machine learning have generated hundreds of candidate drugs, while repurposed agents account for 35% (56 of 158) of drugs and 42% (15 of 36) of Phase 3 agents in the 2026 AD pipeline. Clinical translation, however, remains unproven. Randomised trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists illustrate the gap between prioritisation and therapeutic proof: semaglutide did not slow clinical progression in evoke and evoke+, while liraglutide did not improve the primary FDG-PET endpoint in ELAD. We examine four complementary evidence domains, defining what each can and cannot establish, and position large language models as a cross-cutting tool for evidence synthesis and knowledge-graph reasoning rather than an independent source of biological evidence. Rather than cataloguing methods and candidates, we appraise leading drugs at the individual-molecule level and propose explicit criteria for progression from computational nomination to clinical testing. The framework defines seven requirements for clinical progression: disease-stage matching, adequate site-of-action exposure, including CNS exposure for central mechanisms, mechanistic validation in human-relevant models, biomarker-stratified trial design, convergence across independent evidence domains, causal inference with explicit boundary conditions, and mechanism-aligned endpoints with predefined stopping rules. AI has improved candidate prioritisation in AD, but clinical value will depend on converting ranked hypotheses into pharmacologically plausible and prospectively testable programmes.

title: Astrocyte Biocomputing: Astrocytic Contributions to Neural Network Computation
desc: Conductors are critical for the performance of an orchestra even though they do not emit sound. Basic research and clinical studies in the last decade are revealing that astrocytes may be the "conductors" of the "orchestra" that is the brain network: astrocytes make up approximately $50\%$ of all brain cells but do not emit electrical signals. Nevertheless, they may play critical roles in important cognitive brain functions, specifically learning, memory, and information processing. Here we consider the implications of these discoveries for brain-inspired machine learning (ML), where analogy is typically drawn between neurons and their electrical interactions. We highlight specific algorithms for two key astrocyte characteristics. The first characteristic is the ability to link to and modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously. A model based on this characteristic yields faster training and makes the network more robust to noise, providing a supervised learning algorithm that can be applied to any existing neural network. The second characteristic we focus on is that the non-electrical communication among astrocytes includes slow, rhythmic dynamics. The rhythmic sharing algorithm we developed based on this premise yields rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting. Overall, we find that astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neurocentric algorithms significantly and remediate critical weaknesses of current state-of-the-art ML models.

Artificial intelligence-enhanced electrocardiography for detection and prediction of dilated cardiomyopathy.
desc: [European heart journal] A major challenge in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) care is the identification and management of individuals at risk before disease manifestation. An artificial intelligence (AI) model applied to electrocardiography (ECG) was developed to detect and predict the echocardiographic DCM phenotype (left ventricular dilatation with systolic dysfunction) and was evaluated for its ability to stratify the risk of incident DCM in familial cohorts. A deep learning model was trained to detect the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and to predict its future onset, using more than 330 000 ECG-echocardiogram pairs from the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston. Model performance was validated in cohorts from the UK Biobank, Zhongshan Hospital, and Antwerp University Hospital, and compared with models based on traditional ECG features and echocardiographic traits. To assess performance in familial DCM, genetically predisposed individuals identified through cascade screening at the cardiogenetics clinics of Antwerp University Hospital (n = 166, 18% DCM positive) and Maastricht University Medical Center (n = 177, 18% DCM positive) were evaluated. The AI-ECG model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of .87-.97 for diagnosing the prevalent DCM phenotype, outperforming traditional ECG parameters. AI-ECG was comparable to echocardiography for predicting future DCM (C-index .80-.87 and .80-.90, respectively). In familial cohorts, 5-year negative predictive values were 95.5% (Antwerp) and 91.5% (Maastricht), with corresponding positive predictive values of 42.4% and 39.4%, while high-risk scores were associated with a 5.1-6.4-fold increased risk of incident DCM. The explainable AI-ECG model detects the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and predicts future disease, and supports the exclusion of short- to mid-term disease in genetically at-risk individuals. This low-cost tool could help reduce surveillance burden and facilitate earlier intervention.

title: X-Strata: Separating Aneurysms and Overlapping Vessels into Layers from 2D X-ray Angiography
desc: An X-ray angiogram sums every structure along a ray into one pixel. When vessels cross an aneurysm, they obscure part of it and mix their contrast into its filling curve. We present X-Strata, a network that separates a cine angiogram into three layers: the complete aneurysm sac, the vessels in front of it, and the vessels behind it. Contrast timing indicates how much each layer contributes to a pixel, and parallax between two views indicates their order, which a single view cannot determine. X-Strata first estimates the layers and their contrast curves, then uses the second view to assign vessels to the front or back layer, and lifts all layers into 3D. It learns from layer labels projected from same-session 3D rotational angiography, but needs only 2D cine runs and their acquisition geometry at inference. On 220 held-out patients from three centers (122 external), two-view X-Strata ranks first among 14 baselines, including VGGT and C$^2$RV, in recovering the sac where vessels overlap it (Dice 0.693 internal, 0.641 external) and in ordering the layers (balanced accuracy 0.703, 0.659). Its order accuracy exceeds that of all 11 end-to-end baselines by at least 4.1 points internally and 3.3 externally (Holm-adjusted $p < 0.001$) and grows with view separation. Recovered 3D sac surfaces have a median Chamfer distance of 0.34 mm on the internal cohort. X-Strata may therefore provide layered aneurysm and vessel information, including 3D sac shape, for patients who undergo only 2D angiography.
