Artificial Intelligence for Colorectal Cancer Diagnosis: A Comprehensive Survey of Modalities, Frameworks, and Clinical Tasks.
desc: [Cancers] The diagnosis of colorectal cancer encompasses nine complementary modalities: stool-based screening, blood-based biomarkers, cross-sectional imaging, endoscopic evaluation, histopathology, liquid biopsy, molecular and genetic profiling, microbiome analysis, and nanotechnology-based diagnostics. This narrative review synthesizes 160 references spanning seven task-specific artificial intelligence domains, including computer-aided detection, optical diagnosis, invasion depth prediction, computational pathology and radiogenomics, metastasis forecasting, neoadjuvant treatment response prediction, and surgical workflow analysis. We propose a conceptual multimodal pipeline comprising data ingestion, preprocessing and harmonization, feature representation, multimodal fusion, forecasting, explainability, and validation. A structured evidence grading framework classifies each clinical task by evidence level, consistency, and clinical readiness. We further catalog public datasets, challenge benchmarks, and five reporting standards: TRIPOD-AI, CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, DECIDE-AI, and CLAIM. Computer-aided detection and optical diagnosis demonstrate the highest maturity with Level 1 evidence from randomized controlled trials, while computational pathology, radiogenomics, and metastasis prediction remain at Level 2 with retrospective validation (internal or external). Microbiome screening, nanotechnology diagnostics, and surgical phase recognition are exploratory. The principal barriers to clinical adoption are domain shift, data scarcity, calibration, prospective validation, and workflow integration. We conclude that clinically useful artificial intelligence requires robust external validation, uncertainty quantification, explainable outputs, standardized reporting, and a structured translational pathway from retrospective evidence through regulatory clearance to post-deployment monitoring.

title: QCAP-VQA: Question-Conditioned Capped Prior-Mass Supervision for Medical Visual Question Answering
desc: Medical visual question answering models can answer correctly without attending to the anatomy that the question names. Automatic region priors allow spatial supervision without expert masks, but they are noisy, and it is unclear how strongly they should shape attention and how their effect should be verified. We present QCAP-VQA, which supervises a subset of cross-attention heads with a question-conditioned prior built from ranked segmentation proposals. Its capped prior-mass objective penalizes insufficient attention inside the prior only below a threshold. We evaluate attention against SLAKE structure boxes that play no role in training, separating attention on the named anatomy from how attention shifts between questions about the same image. QCAP-VQA matches the accuracy of a baseline without spatial supervision (84.26% vs. 84.23%), and every evaluated prior-supervised model places more attention on the annotated structures. Over a 64-fold range of regularization strength, the capped objective keeps prior mass between 0.67 and 0.77, whereas a pooled region-mass objective drives it to 0.97 and loses accuracy. The cost lies in question conditioning: as the constraint widens or strengthens, attention shifts agree less with the expert-defined contrast. Across 13 configurations, prior-referenced and expert-referenced evaluation rank the models in largely opposite order (Spearman correlation of -0.87), and the capped models it favors track the prior's own errors. Because clinical use of medical visual question answering requires answers grounded in the queried anatomy, supervision from automatic priors should be judged against independent anatomical references.

title: Implementing Artificial Intelligence in Daily Clinical Practice, from Voice Dictation to Operating Room Organization: A Targeted Narrative Review with Hysteroscopy as a Clinical Exemplar.
desc: [Journal of clinical medicine] Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering routine care through documentation tools, decision support, and hospital operations. The central question is whether these systems improve clinical work and patient care once embedded in routine workflows, not only whether they perform well on test data. This targeted narrative review follows AI from voice dictation and ambient documentation to operating room (OR) organization, using hysteroscopy as a clinical exemplar of the transition from technical performance to clinical utility. Evidence identified through targeted searches completed on 6 September 2026 was appraised with a framework that distinguishes image-level from patient-level results, internal from independent validation, and discrimination from clinical utility. Randomized trials and multisite observational data show modest, product-dependent benefits of clinician-reviewed ambient documentation; inaccuracies persist. Evidence for patient-message drafting derives from ratings of responses to public-forum questions and supports only bounded, supervised feasibility testing. In hysteroscopy, selected models discriminate well in narrowly defined tasks, but most studies are retrospective, image-level, or internally validated, and patient-level errors in high-risk categories are seldom reported. Reported gains in OR scheduling come largely from simulation. Safe implementation requires a defined clinical need, baseline measurement, subgroup-aware local validation, accountable review, and predefined criteria for expansion or withdrawal.

title: More Genes, Faster Inference: Efficient Large-Panel Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology
desc: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) prediction from histology aims to infer spatially resolved gene expression profiles directly from tissue images. This is a challenging problem that is currently often addressed with complicated model architectures, additional inputs, and complicated training procedures, while remaining limited to fixed, small gene panels. This raises a natural question: Is there an efficient method for large-panel ST prediction? Here, we present GeneFlow, a simpler yet effective framework for large-scale spatial gene expression prediction that unifies flow-matching generative modeling with structured multimodal fusion. Specifically, GeneFlow first encodes both histological morphology and cross-gene interactions in spatial spots through histology and gene tokenizers. The model directly predicts spatial gene expression, rather than an intermediate velocity field, while being trained with a velocity-based flow-matching objective. We show that, even without relying on heavy generative pipelines, GeneFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple ST benchmarks, with up to 56.8% gains in 1,000-gene prediction. Extensive experiments further show that GeneFlow produces biologically meaningful spot profiles while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude, thereby improving efficiency and scalability, particularly in clinical settings. We believe GeneFlow provides an opportunity for leveraging widely available histology images for downstream biological discovery. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZZhangsm/GeneFlow

title: Multimodal Risk Stratification and Surveillance for Gastric Cancer in Chronic Atrophic Gastritis and Gastric Intestinal Metaplasia: Integrating Histology, Endoscopy, Biomarkers, and Artificial Intelligence.
desc: [Clinical and experimental gastroenterology] Gastric cancer remains a major global health burden, and chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG) and gastric intestinal metaplasia (GIM) are important premalignant conditions. The risk of progression, however, varies considerably between individuals, making reliable risk stratification central to decisions on surveillance. Histological staging remains the most established approach. In a recent meta-analysis of prospective cohorts, Operative Link on Gastritis Assessment (OLGA) stages III-IV and OLGIM (Operative Link on Gastric Intestinal Metaplasia Assessment) stages III-IV were associated with substantially higher risks of gastric cancer than stages 0-II, with risk ratios of 32.31 and 12.38, respectively. Endoscopic assessment adds information on the distribution of mucosal abnormalities and can improve biopsy targeting; an EGGIM score >4 has shown 95.7% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity for identifying OLGIM stages III-IV. Helicobacter pylori eradication reduces subsequent gastric cancer risk, but surveillance remains necessary in patients with advanced atrophy, extensive GIM, or previous gastric neoplasia. Serological biomarkers may help identify individuals who should undergo endoscopy, although variation in assay thresholds and population characteristics limits their use for definitive risk staging. Artificial intelligence is also being explored to improve diagnostic consistency. In a multicentre pathology study, a deep-learning model achieved external-test AUCs of 0.884 for intestinal metaplasia and 0.877 for atrophy. Current evidence therefore favours combining these approaches according to their clinical roles rather than treating them as interchangeable tools: histology remains the basis of risk staging, endoscopy refines mucosal assessment and biopsy, biomarkers are most useful for triage, and artificial intelligence may support interpretation. Whether such integrated strategies improve surveillance efficiency or clinical outcomes still requires prospective, externally validated studies.

title: Electrocardiographic Imaging via Posterior Sampling under Operator Discrepancy
desc: Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface potentials, an ill-posed inverse problem. Diffusion posterior samplers combine a learned prior with an explicit forward operator that they assume to be accurate. In ECGI this operator is only an estimate, because the body changes with respiration and posture, and body composition such as subcutaneous fat is rarely known for an individual patient. The resulting operator discrepancy is structured and depends on the heart signal. We introduce OpDis-PS, a diffusion posterior sampler that models this discrepancy instead of treating it as signal-independent noise. OpDis-PS learns how the discrepancy depends on the signal, folds this into a corrected forward operator, and reconstructs with a fixed prior across all operator conditions. We study two realistic sources of discrepancy, changing lung conductivity and an added subcutaneous-fat layer. Across both, OpDis-PS reconstructs more accurately than classical regularization and learned predictors, with its largest gains on held-out cardiac pathologies.

title: Performance of a Large Language Model for Predicting Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes in Knee Osteoarthritis: Single-Center Prospective Observational Study.
desc: [JMIR medical informatics] Large language models (LLMs) can extract information from unstructured clinical text, but it remains unclear whether their ability to assess current status translates into reliable predictions of longitudinal outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate DeepSeek's ability to assess baseline clinical and radiographic status in knee osteoarthritis (KOA), its performance in predicting 6-month outcomes, and its interrun reproducibility. This study used a single-center, prospective observational cohort design to conduct a blinded, retrospective evaluation of the LLM. A total of 128 patients with primary KOA were enrolled, of whom 111 (86.7%) completed the 6-month follow-up and were included in the primary analysis. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and a rheumatologist independently assessed KOA diagnoses, baseline Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) scores, and Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grading based on the same standardized interview records and imaging reports and predicted 6-month outcomes. The LLM was run independently 3 times. The actual outcomes determined by another senior physician served as the reference, and the results were compared with the physician's predictions and the persistence model. The LLM showed high baseline diagnostic agreement with the physician (105/111, 94.6%) and good agreement on the WOMAC and KL, but 6-month predictions (WOMAC mean absolute error=5.92-6.58; KL exact agreement=74/111, 66.7%-76/111, 68.5%) were worse than those of the physician comparator (mean absolute error=3.86; 96/111, 86.5%) and not superior to those of the persistence model (mean absolute error=5.43). Despite high interrun intraclass correlation coefficients (0.982 and 0.965), exact agreement between runs was poor (35/111, 31.5% and 7/111, 6.3%). The evaluated DeepSeek configuration may support structured baseline KOA assessment. However, its 6-month predictive accuracy and patient-level stability remain limited. Prognostic applications require evidence of added value over a persistence model.

title: Where to Predict in Retinal OCT? Anatomy-Guided Target Selection for I-JEPA
desc: Self-supervised learning aims to learn meaningful representations from unlabeled data, potentially allowing models to capture subtle anatomical variations across patients and reduce the amount of labeled data needed. Image-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA) learns by predicting target-region representations from visible context rather than reconstructing pixels. However, its uniform target placement does not account for the anatomical structure of retinal OCT, where retinal tissue occupies only part of each B-scan. We investigate anatomy-guided target selection using image intensity and predicted retinal segmentation while retaining the I-JEPA architecture and latent prediction objective. We compare anatomy-guided rectangular targets, anatomy-shaped targets and coverage-constrained placement with uniform masking, and evaluate the learned representations using linear probing for glaucoma classification on FairVision. We found that rectangular targets guided by image intensity achieved the highest linear-probe AUC in our comparisons. We show that anatomically meaningful target selection is promising for retinal OCT representation learning, while greater anatomical specificity did not consistently improve performance.

title: ChatGPT-related research in medical education: A dual-database bibliometric review and science-mapping analysis, 2023 to 2026.
desc: [Medicine] The medical-education literature on ChatGPT has grown rapidly since 2023, but bibliometric patterns vary with database coverage, indexing fields, and the boundary used to define educational relevance. We examined publication growth, collaboration, and thematic development and assessed whether the leading patterns were stable under a stricter topic definition. Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and PubMed were searched on September 5, 2026; the PubMed publication-date filter extended through September 4, 2026. WoSCC supported citation- and Author Keyword-based science mapping, whereas PubMed provided a complementary Medical Subject Headings-based view. The expanded corpora contained 665 WoSCC and 1106 PubMed records, with strict topic-specific subsets of 532 and 898 records, respectively. Bibliometrix/R, VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and Microsoft Excel were used for descriptive bibliometrics, collaboration networks, thematic mapping, multiple correspondence analysis, keyword co-occurrence, Trend Topics, burst detection, and journal mapping. Data from 2026 were treated as partial-year observations. WoSCC publication output increased from 66 records in 2023 to 169 in 2024 and 242 in 2025; 188 records were indexed during the partial 2026 period. The United States had the largest corresponding-author output, and Sichuan University was the leading displayed affiliation. The keyword structure centered on medical education, ChatGPT, artificial intelligence, and large language models. CiteSpace identified 9 keyword clusters, including medical education, large language models, medical students, generative artificial intelligence, prompt engineering, clinical decision-making, and patient education. Recently emerging terms included DeepSeek, clinical reasoning, and anatomy education. Author Keyword rankings were highly concordant between the expanded and strict WoSCC datasets (Spearman ρ = 0.973, P < .001). ChatGPT-related medical-education research expanded substantially after 2023 and diversified across assessment, clinical reasoning, educational applications, and broader LLM-related themes. The leading WoSCC keyword structure remained stable under the stricter topic definition. WoSCC and PubMed captured different bibliographic features and are best interpreted as complementary sources.

title: Continuous Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation Using PPG From Methods to Clinical Translation
desc: Continuous blood pressure (BP) monitoring could improve hypertension management by capturing changes that intermittent cuff measurements miss. Photoplethysmography (PPG) is widely explored for cuffless BP estimation because optical sensors are inexpensive, wearable, and already present in many consumer and clinical devices. PPG, however, does not measure arterial pressure: BP is inferred from waveform characteristics or pulse timing, which also depend on vascular tone, arterial stiffness, sensor contact, motion, and individual physiology. This survey reviews PPG-based cuffless BP estimation along the full measurement chain, covering physiological mechanisms, waveform features, pulse arrival time (PAT), pulse transit time (PTT), machine-learning methods, datasets, calibration, validation, deployment, bias, and clinical translation. Studies are assessed by the strength of evidence they provide rather than by reported error alone, with particular attention to subject and temporal leakage, dataset imbalance, calibration dependence and drift, motion artifacts, and the gap between benchmark accuracy and reliable real-world measurement. The review finds that progress depends on more than better prediction algorithms. Future work should prioritize physiologically informed models, diverse longitudinal datasets, transparent reporting of calibration requirements and failure rates, stronger evaluation protocols, and studies that demonstrate practical value in clinical care.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Heart Failure: Early Detection, Phenotyping, and Prognostic Modeling.
desc: [Methodist DeBakey cardiovascular journal] This review examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) across the heart failure (HF) continuum, with particular emphasis on patient identification and early recognition, AI-enabled electrocardiography and echocardiography, etiologic and phenotypic classification, electronic health record-based staging and risk prediction, advanced HF identification, continuous monitoring, treatment optimization, and emerging applications of agentic AI.

title: Alignment with Reflect-Reasoning: Learning How To Follow Principles
desc: The appropriate governing norms and principles for the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) often depend on cultural context and deployment application. However, most alignment techniques focus on training models to conform to human preferences or constitutional principles specified at training time and subsequently fixed. In practice, many deployers rely on system prompting to implement contextual norms and guardrails at inference time. Prior work has shown that post-generation reflective reasoning with critique and revision can improve conformance compared to simple system prompting, but such methods are limited to the reasoning abilities inherent in the trained model. We introduce Reflect-Reasoning, a training method that teaches models how to reason about alignment to principles, rather than simply which principles to follow. Across five models, Reflect-Reasoning consistently outperforms both system prompting and explicit prompting strategies for in-context reflective reasoning. These improvements extend and generalize to entirely out-of-distribution domains of medical and financial principles. We additionally demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning reduces the occurrence of rare but serious principle violations. Finally, we show that Reflect-Reasoning does not erode the safety engineering of a model and is robust against jailbreaking attempts using adversarial constitutions. Overall, our results demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning is a scalable method for training constitutional alignment as a generalizable reasoning capability, enabling models to adapt to novel principles and produce transparent reasoning traces without additional fine-tuning.

title: A comprehensive study of skin lesion segmentation and classification using deep learning techniques.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Deep learning has become an important computational approach in dermatology because it enables automated segmentation and classification of skin lesions. Manual dermoscopic analysis is time-consuming and depends on specialist expertise, with potential inter-observer variability. There is a need to develop reliable computer-aided diagnostic tools. This structured narrative review covers journal papers published mainly from 2018 to 2026 on skin lesion analysis with focus on image preprocessing, benchmark datasets, conventional machine learning approaches, convolutional neural networks, U-Net architectures, transfer learning approaches, Vision Transformers, attention-based models, ensemble solutions, and hybrid segmentation-classification systems. Building on present reviews covering individual tasks as well as broader segmentation-classification pipelines, the present work provides a critical development-to-deployment analysis connecting dataset characteristics, preprocessing, segmentation, classification, evaluation, explainability, robustness, fairness, computational requirements, and clinical applicability. The paper describes widely used evaluation metrics and explains why results obtained across different datasets, partitions, and experimental setups should not be directly compared. Major open problems include class imbalance, data bias, domain shift, limited representation of diverse skin tones, inadequate external validation, computational requirements, and limited explainability of efficient models. Emerging trends such as self-supervised learning, Transformers, foundation models, explainable AI, federated learning, and multi-modal clinical data are reviewed as well. The review offers practical advice to researchers and clinicians on how to approach the preprocessing, segmentation, classification, and evaluation of skin lesions and highlights priorities in developing clinically reliable skin lesion analysis systems.

title: AI Applications in Aortic and Peripheral Artery Disease: Risk Prediction, Imaging, Procedural Support, and Longitudinal Surveillance.
desc: [Methodist DeBakey cardiovascular journal] Aortic disease and lower-extremity peripheral artery disease (PAD) generate substantial morbidity, mortality, and longitudinal imaging burden. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly studied for vascular risk prediction, image analysis, procedural support, and surveillance, but the maturity of these applications is heterogeneous. This review evaluates recent AI applications in aortic disease and PAD, emphasizing the distinction between algorithmic performance, external validation, demonstrated workflow impact, and proven patient benefit. Automated image segmentation and opportunistic abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) detection have the most mature evidence base, including retrospective external validation and, for AI-assisted AAA case finding, nonrandomized evidence of improved downstream evaluation and follow-up. Conversely, while machine-learning models for vascular risk prediction and disease progression often report high retrospective accuracy, their clinical readiness remains strictly investigational. Across most aortic and PAD applications, there is a persistent lack of independent external validation, decision-curve analysis, and prospective testing against standard care. Image-fusion guidance has clinical evidence for reducing procedural resource use, but this evidence should not be conflated with autonomous AI or robotic navigation. Cardiovascular digital twins remain largely mechanistic, computational, or early-development frameworks. AI can augment vascular imaging and risk assessment, but high retrospective accuracy is not equivalent to clinical utility. Current guideline thresholds for repair, revascularization, and surveillance should not be altered on the basis of investigational radiomics or prediction models. Translation requires multicenter external validation, prospective workflow evaluation, calibration and net-benefit assessment, transparent reporting, and trials demonstrating improved patient outcomes.

title: Personas shift clinical action thresholds in large language models.
desc: [npj health systems] Clinical large language model (LLM) deployment is shifting from feasibility to liability, while current guidance largely treats model behavior as a control problem. We tested whether decision-style system prompts shift clinical action thresholds when clinical facts are held constant, and whether these shifts are consistent across settings and models. We defined nine physician personas by crossing three ethical orientations (duty-based, care-based, utilitarian) with three cognitive styles (intuitive, integrative, analytic). Twenty open-weight LLMs were evaluated on 2500 simulated emergency department vignettes and 2500 MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries. For each text, models answered five binary decision items (safety, autonomy, treatment, resource use, follow-up). Each condition was repeated ten times, yielding 5,000,000 total decisions. Under baseline prompting, models answered "Yes" to 42.8% of decisions. Persona prompts shifted affirmative rates from 36.9% to 46.4%, a 9.5 percentage-point swing under fixed clinical evidence. Effects were largest in autonomy and treatment and were consistent across corpora (85.7% directional agreement; r = 0.82 for effect sizes). Susceptibility varied by model (4.9-16.1 points), with no consistent protection from medical fine-tuning or model size. Decision-style system prompts reliably change clinical action thresholds in LLMs under fixed evidence. Prompting is a policy-setting layer, not just a communication layer, and should be treated as a first-class deployment configuration.

title: In silico drug discovery framework leveraging biomedical foundation models and evaluating generative models-a use case on 3CLpro.
source: PubMed · Journal of computer-aided molecular design
desc: [Journal of computer-aided molecular design] AI models such as foundation models and generative models have shown promise for aiding drug discovery alongside traditional cheminformatics and bioinformatics tools and physics-based approaches. In this study, we design a workflow that integrates these AI methods to generate molecules alongside established informatic and predictive filtering approaches to streamline downselection of molecules from the massive and noisy result sets generated by AI. This workflow evaluates generative methods based on validity, reliability, diversity, similarity, hallucination and campaign needs. Analyses are made on the original proprietary dataset to determine molecular property thresholds for screening criteria. Overall, 249 molecules are selected from ~ 5 million generated molecules. 18 molecules are then validated with free energy perturbation simulations. 5 out of 5 retain on target inhibition, with IC50 values below 1 μM. 1 of the 5 experimentally validated molecules displayed greater inhibition than the corresponding lead molecule. Predictive foundation model MMELON yields Pearson correlation R = 0.72 in blind test, showing potential for future drug discovery campaigns.

title: Artificial intelligence and clinical reasoning - a qualitative study with general practice trainees in Germany.
desc: [BMC medical education] General practitioners face high complexity in clinical decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) may support clinical reasoning, but their impact on decision-making processes and postgraduate medical training remains unclear. This qualitative study aims to explore General Practice (GP) trainee's use of LLMs in clinical reasoning and their educational needs. GP trainees were recruited and interviewed with semi-structured interview-guide. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed qualitatively. Seventeen GP trainees participated (mean interview duration: 38 min; range: 21-63 min). AI was perceived as a tool to augment and accelerate clinical decision-making, while potential risks of deskilling were identified. Participants reported a lack of structured AI education and expressed a need for its integration into postgraduate training. Participants perceived AI primarily as a supportive tool that can complement clinical reasoning and improve access to medical knowledge. At the same time, they identified potential risks, including overreliance on AI-generated information and possible effects on the development of clinical expertise. These findings suggest that postgraduate medical training should address AI-related competencies, including critical appraisal, ethical responsibility and appropriate integration of AI into clinical decision-making. AI is already part of clinical practice among GP trainees, offering opportunities to support learning and clinical reasoning while raising concerns about overreliance and critical appraisal. Postgraduate medical training in GP should therefore incorporate structured AI competencies to ensure responsible, reflective and patient-centered use of AI.

title: Artificial Intelligence Models to Predict Recurrence in Patients with Differentiated Thyroid Cancer: A PROBAST + AI Systematic Review of Clinical Applicability.
source: PubMed · Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association
desc: [Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association] Differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) generally carries an excellent prognosis, yet recurrence occurs in up to 8-9% of patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) models are increasingly proposed to predict DTC recurrence; however, their methodological quality and clinical readiness are poorly defined. We conducted a systematic review to evaluate the methodological quality, risk of bias, and applicability of these models using the PROBAST + AI framework. We searched Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane databases, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception to July 13, 2026. Eligible studies included original research developing or validating AI models for recurrence in DTC. Model quality (for development), risk of bias (for evaluation), and applicability were assessed using the PROBAST + AI framework, with a focus on discrimination, calibration, and validation strategies (PROSPERO; registration number [CRD420251004644]). Of 673 records screened, 34 studies were included (21 unique datasets and 13 UCI-derived publications), encompassing 21,267 patients with a recurrence rate of 7.8%. Most were developed in Asian cohorts (17 of 21 datasets) and were structured clinical/tabular variables (82.4%), including demographic, clinical, laboratory, and pathological data, whereas the remaining models incorporated multimodal inputs such as imaging-derived or radiomic features. Notably, nearly one quarter of included studies (13 of 34, 38%) represented reanalysis of a single dataset. Discrimination was reported in 22 of 34 studies (64.7%) (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.67-1.00), though only 10 studies assessed calibration, none with standardized metrics. The PROBAST + AI assessment revealed high overall quality concerns in 26 of 34 (76.5%) development studies due to reliance on single-center cohorts, inadequate handling of missing data, and absence of external validation. Only 6 of 34 included studies (17.6%) were judged to have low overall quality concern, whereas 17 of 34 (50.0%) were rated as having low applicability concern. AI models for predicting DTC recurrence show promising discriminatory performance but have substantial methodological shortcomings in development, and a lack of calibration and external validation necessary for clinical use. Given the guidelines' emphasis on risk-adapted de-escalation of therapy, the development of robust, validated, and clinically calibrated AI tools is a priority. Current evidence remains insufficient to supp

title: AI-assisted literature mining of perovskite ink formulations using a hybrid regex-LLM extraction pipeline.
desc: [RSC advances] Reproducibility of perovskite solar cell and LED fabrication depends critically on ink formulation details that are typically buried in the Methods sections of scientific articles. Manual curation of such data is slow, inconsistent, and does not scale. Here we present an end-to-end automated AI-assisted pipeline that (i) queries the OpenAlex academic graph to identify open-access publications containing perovskite ink formulations, (ii) downloads and parses PDF full texts using rule-based regex extraction, (iii) applies a large language model (LLM, Claude Haiku 4.5) as a second extraction layer to recover structured perovskite formulas, cleaned molarity values, and novel additive chemistries missed by regex, (iv) assigns a multi-criteria confidence score to each extracted recipe, and (v) exports a structured, analysis-ready dataset in tidy format. Applied to a corpus of 1041 screened publications, the pipeline recovered 68 annotated ink formulations from 71 successfully retrieved PDFs. The LLM extraction layer identified 46 structured perovskite formulas (31 unique compositions, including mixed-cation and quasi-2D types), increased molarity coverage from 49% to 60%, and increased high-confidence extractions from 32 (regex, score ≥7) to 36 (LLM confidence = high). Twenty records are automatically promoted and manually validated as the GOLD standard. The published data encompass 44 publication venues, and research articles published between 2014 and 2025, which record solvent systems, precursor stoichiometry, molarity, and additive solvent chemistry of halide perovskite inks. All code and data are freely available to accelerate materials informatics in this field.

title: Design and Simulation of an AI-Powered Artificial Pancreas System With Personalized Glucose Sensing and Insulin Delivery.
desc: [Artificial organs] Achieving tight glycemic control in Type 1 diabetes is challenged by non-linear metabolic dynamics and insulin-stacking risk. Artificial intelligence models offer improved personalization, but their opacity raises safety concerns, particularly for basal insulin dosing, which is often treated as static in existing decision-support systems. We propose a hybrid closed-loop system combining a data-driven LightGBM regressor for basal dose prediction, trained on the T1D-UOM dataset, with a physiologically grounded, rule-based safety layer at the edge. Basal insulin is predicted from cyclical time encoding and glucose rate-of-change; bolus dosing follows carbohydrate intake and correction requirements. A time-bounded insulin-on-board model, an uncertainty-adaptive post-bolus damping factor, and a predictive low-glucose-suspend rule reproducing the Tandem Basal-IQ protocol together suspend or reduce delivery when residual insulin is high or hypoglycemia is projected. The system was evaluated in silico over 60 continuous days under shadow-mode replay and closed-loop reduced-order simulation, including an ablation with bolus delivery suppressed. Under chronological, within-subject validation, the offline basal estimator achieved R 2 = 0.68 and MAE = 0.21 U; under strict leave-one-subject-out validation on the same real cohort, performance did not generalize to unseen subjects ( R 2 = - 0.49 , MAE = 0.49 U). The hybrid controller maintained Time-in-Range at 62.8% within the reduced-order closed-loop simulation, with no violations of the insulin-on-board suspension or damping rules; suppressing bolus delivery in an ablation within this simulation dropped Time-in-Range to 26.1%, indicating that, within the reduced-order model, bolus delivery is a determinant of simulated glycemic outcome. The proposed architecture demonstrates a safety-audited template for combining machine-learning basal prediction with clinically grounded dosing rules. Validation on real outcome data and physical hardware is identified as the next steps toward clinical translation.

title: The Potential of Large Language Models in Gynecologic Oncology Telephone Triage.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Introduction: Nurse-led telephone triage, frequently guided by the United Kingdom Oncology Nursing Society (UKONS) tool, is a cornerstone of supportive oncology care, yet the appropriateness of triage decisions varies across settings. Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in medical communication but remain unvalidated for autonomous clinical decision-making, particularly in gynecologic oncology, where remote and telephone-based care pose distinct challenges. Methods and Materials: Twenty fictitious case vignettes representing common treatment-related toxicities in gynecologic oncology were developed. Three board-certified gynecologic consultants independently assigned UKONS Red-Amber-Green (RAG) triage categories, reaching unanimous consensus that served as the reference standard. Vignettes were submitted verbatim, as single-turn queries with no follow-up prompting, to three publicly available LLMs (OpenEvidence, ChatGPT, Google Gemini). LLM responses were mapped to RAG categories and compared descriptively against the reference standard, stratified by treatment type and platform. Results: All three LLMs achieved 100% concordance with the reference standard for all Red cases across both treatment groups, with no high-acuity case downgraded to self-care. Discrepancies clustered at lower-acuity boundaries. In the chemotherapy-alone group, errors were limited to omission of an explicit 24-h follow-up window for 1 Amber-rated complaints. In the combined group, all LLMs over-triaged intermediate-risk complaints toward immediate or same-day evaluation; low-risk complaints showed more variable over-triage. Conclusions: LLMs identified unambiguous emergent gynecologic oncology symptoms, preserving the UKONS safety floor, but showed relatively reduced precision and a conservative over-triage bias at lower-acuity margins, especially in the combined-therapy collective. These findings support a supervised, adjunctive role for LLMs, rather than autonomous deployment, pending prospective validation.

title: Unlocking Power of Medical Research.
source: PubMed · Journal of obstetrics and gynaecology of India
desc: [Journal of obstetrics and gynaecology of India] The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), New Delhi, convened a half-day symposium on July 22, 2026, with the theme "Medical Publishing in the Era of AI and Anti-Science - Navigating Challenges, Fostering Integrity." The program included keynote addresses and three panel discussions featuring editors, publishers, and journalists.

title: Dendritic structure enables powerful plasticity.
desc: [Current research in neurobiology] Over the past decades, it has become increasingly clear that the complex morphology of cortical neurons is more than just a quirk of evolution, and that dendritic compartments serve as computational elements in their own right, rather than just providing connections between nerve cell bodies. While most computational studies discuss the enhanced representational capabilities of multi-compartment models as compared to point neurons, we focus here on the implications of neuronal morphology for synaptic plasticity. We argue that the ability of single neurons to simultaneously encode multiple pieces of information gives synapses local access to more than just the classical Hebbian pre- and postsynaptic terms, and with much greater specificity and reaction speed than permitted by other globally modulated factors. Based on a comparative review of recent dendritic learning models, we show how such neuronal compartmentalization can provide synapses with the means for calculating various forms of error signals, which in turn give rise to powerful real-time and fully local instantiations of deep learning through gradient descent. Implemented within cortical microcircuits capable of propagating and manipulating these errors, compartmentalized neurons thus ultimately enable the learning of far more complex tasks than are achievable by globally modulated Hebbian plasticity alone.

title: The Europe-Asia-Pacific Divide in Atrial Fibrillation Management: Evidence, Practice, and Policy.
desc: [JACC. Asia] Atrial fibrillation affects approximately 60 million people worldwide, and Europe and the Asia-Pacific region together carry most of that burden. This state-of-the-art review compares the 2 regions across 6 domains: epidemiology and risk factors, lifestyle and comorbidity management, stroke prevention, rhythm control and catheter ablation, digital health and artificial intelligence-electrocardiogram, and health system infrastructure and policy. Practice diverges in all 6. European management follows European Society of Cardiology guidelines, whereas Asia-Pacific region care varies across socioeconomic settings and rests on population-scale evidence, with region-wide guidance so far limited to topic-specific Asia Pacific Heart Rhythm Society (APHRS) consensus statements until the first APHRS guideline was released in 2026. Anticoagulation gaps have narrowed in both regions, yet disparities in financing, electrophysiology capacity, and digital access persist, and differences within each region rival those between them. Closing these gaps requires region-specific, resource-adapted strategies and mutual adoption of evidence generated in each region.

title: Decoding metabolic bottlenecks: Advanced technologies for key gene identification in microbial cell factories.
desc: [Biotechnology advances] Constructing efficient microbial cell factories is a crucial platform for the industrial production of high-value-added products, and precisely identifying the key genes that govern biosynthesis levels is a core step in overcoming productivity bottlenecks. However, due to the extensive and complex regulatory networks inherent in biological systems, accurately identifying these key genes has long posed substantial challenges. This review systematically summarizes two main technical routes currently used to identify key genes: prior-knowledge-guided prediction methods and phenotype-oriented screening approaches. On this basis, we compare the applicable scenarios and limitations of each technique. Subsequently, we highlight the enabling role of machine learning in key genes prediction, particularly its value in functional gene annotation and the construction of genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs). We also summarize the progress and potential improvements in multi-target iterative engineering tools. The integration and synergistic application of these technologies can effectively accelerate the iterative Design-Build-Test-Learn (DBTL) cycle, thereby providing a methodological foundation for the rational design and efficient engineering of next-generation microbial cell factories.

title: From Quality Detection to Intelligent Management: A Mechanism-Informed Framework Integrating Foodomics, Microbiome Science and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Fish Flesh Quality.
desc: [Foods (Basel, Switzerland)] Fish flesh quality is a multidimensional phenotype shaped across the production-post-harvest continuum by interacting metabolic, structural, lipid, redox, and microbial processes. Conventional sensory, physicochemical, biochemical, and instrumental measurements remain essential for defining quality phenotypes, while foodomics and microbiome approaches increasingly resolve the biological mechanisms underlying quality formation and deterioration. This review integrates recent advances in fish flesh quality assessment, foodomics, microbiome science, intelligent sensing, machine learning, and explainable artificial intelligence from a mechanism-informed perspective. Particular emphasis is placed on energy metabolism, lipid remodeling, redox regulation, muscle-fiber and collagen organization, microbial metabolites, and spoilage-related microbial functions that connect biological state with measurable quality traits. We further examine the transition from current-state recognition toward prospective quality prediction, with emphasis on biological interpretability, transferability, external validation, and uncertainty. Building on this evidence, we propose a dual-stage framework in which a context-dependent harvest biological-state vector integrates energetic, structural, lipid/nutritional, redox, and product-associated microbial dimensions to connect pre-harvest quality formation with post-harvest deterioration trajectories. Together, these advances provide a basis for moving from quality detection toward prospective prediction and mechanism-informed intelligent management of fish flesh quality.

title: AI and the Responsibility-Bearing Status of Authorship.
desc: [Philosophy & technology] Generative AI has sharpened an old question: who, or what, can be an author? The central aim of this paper is to reconstruct the conception of authorship already implicit in copyright law. I argue that copyright encodes authorship as a responsibility-bearing status, constituted by a cluster of conditions: intentional agency, guided control, and relational expression (ACE). The paper's contribution is to make that conception explicit, to show that the human-authorship rule is best understood as a proxy for those capacities, not a species predicate, and to explain why this generates a tension with recognizing current generative AI systems as authors unless one is prepared to attribute to them the thicker agential capacities ACE requires. On that basis, the paper also clarifies why AI-assisted works may still be human-authored, while some AI-generated outputs give rise to genuine authorship gaps.
